:::{.callout-tip .objectives #objectives-0601}

#### Learning objectives
By the end of this part of the practical you will be able to:

* Understand what functions are and when they are used. 
* Write functions to automate aspects of your analysis.
* Use a function to run a multi-step analysis on a data frame.

:::

In this practical, you will need two Quarto documents:

* `prac6_exercises.qmd` for basic exercises
* `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` for an analysis of the mutations associated with different types of cancer.

## The dataset {#sec-dataset06}

Today we will work with data from [The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)](https://www.cancer.gov/ccg/research/genome-sequencing/tcga), a **cancer genomics** research project in which collected and analysed thousands of matched pairs of tumour and normal tissue samples from the same individuals, across 33 types of cancer. The samples were compared in terms of their genome, transcriptome, epigenome and proteome.

![The Cancer Genome Atlas](images/TCGA.png){#fig-tcga}

We will focus on the **genome** data, and specifically on mutations identified in the cancer samples. These mutations have been identified using a panel of seven different computational tools as being significantly enriched in tumour tissue compared to normal tissue. The methodology used to define these mutations is [described here](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2018.03.002). The data were used as a starting point for this [landmark publication](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.02.060), in which 299 cancer driver genes were identified.

You have been provided with **31 CSV files** (two of the cancer types, rectal adenocarcinoma and colon adenocarcinoma are merged as colorectal adenocarcinoma in the publicly available data, and one, acute myeloid leukaemia, had no mutations which meet our criteria), each representing one type of cancer. 

Each data frame lists all of the genes in which mutations were identified in at least 10% of people with that particular cancer type. Severe mutations are defined here as insertions, deletions, splice site mutations and non-synonymous mutations.

The columns are as follows:

* `Gene`: [HUGO](https://www.genenames.org/) name for the gene.
* `Cancer_Type`: The type of cancer described in this file.
* `Gene_Mutation_Count`: Number of mutations identified in this gene in this cancer type, including multiple mutations in the same gene in one individual.
* `Gene_Severe_Mutation_Count`: Number of severe mutations identified in this gene in this cancer type, including multiple mutations in the same gene in one individual.
* `Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Count`: Number of individuals with at least one mutation in this gene in this cancer type.
* `Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count`: Number of individuals with at least one severe mutation in this gene in this cancer type.


## Writing functions {#sec-writing_functions}

In the practical course so far, we have used many of the different **functions** (see @sec-functions) which are built into R and provided by additional packages.

However, it is also possible to **write your own functions**. This means you can use the same set of instructions multiple times, possibly with different inputs. This will be very useful for this practical, as we have 31 files to process.

Functions have several advantages:

* Using the same code again saves time.
* If you want to change something in the code, you only have to change it once.
* Because you are writing less code, you are less likely to make mistakes.

Here is a simple example of a function, to calculate the equivalent age of a dog if it were a human, its age in *dog years*. According to [the BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/magazine-22479412), for a medium dog the calculation is:

$$
d = 21 + \left(4 \times (\text{h} - 2)\right)
$$

Where *d* is the age in dog years and *h* is age in human years.

We can write a function to calculate this. We define a function using the function `function()`. It is best to give the function a descriptive name.

The steps of the function are then written in curly brackets (`{}`) on the following lines.

The `return` statement defines what the **output** of the function will be.

```{r first_function}
human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
```

So here we are saying:

* <code>[human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years)]{.orange-text}</code>: I am defining a function, it is called `human_years_to_dog_years` and takes one argument, `age_in_human_years`.
* <code>[{]{.orange-text}</code>: Here are the steps.
* <code>[age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))]{.orange-text}</code>: Run this equation on the variable `age_in_human_years` and store the result as the variable `age_in_dog_years`.
* <code>[return (age_in_dog_years)]{.orange-text}</code>: Return the value of the variable `age_in_dog_years` as the output of the function
* <code>[}]{.orange-text}</code>: That's all.

Let's use our function to calculate the age in dog years of some dogs.

Monty is 6 in human years.

```{r dog_age_1}
print(human_years_to_dog_years(6))
```


Noodle is 2 in human years:

```{r dog_age_2}
print(human_years_to_dog_years(2))
```

We can also apply our function to a column in a data frame.

Let's say we have this data frame of dogs.

```{r dog_tibble}
dog_data <- tibble(
  Name = c(
    "Biscuit",
    "Snowball",
    "Pickle",
    "Artemis",
    "Bert"
  ),
  Age_Human_Years = c(6, 1, 12, 4, 15)
)
gt(dog_data)
```

Using our `human_years_to_dog_years()` function, we can calculate the age in dog years of each dog.

[comment]: todo_katy link to the mutate explanation once I've written it.

::: {.callout-note #note-mutate}

Remember that the `mutate()` function allows us to create a new column in a data frame by applying a function to an existing column.
:::

```{r dog_years_df}
dog_data_updated <- dog_data |>
  mutate(Age_Dog_Years = human_years_to_dog_years(Age_Human_Years))

gt(dog_data_updated)
```


There are two important things to learn about functions:

**1. In order to run the function, you need to call it**

So, if I just run this code:

```{r function_call_1}
human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
```

R now knows this function exists, but it hasn't been used yet.

If we want to actually run it, we need to add a **function call**.

```{r function_call_2}
human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
# function call
print(human_years_to_dog_years(10))
```


**2. Variables you create inside a function only exist inside the function.**

So, the following will work - inside the function, between the curly brackets, we can access the variable `age_in_dog_years`.

```{r function_vars1}
human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  print(paste("Age in human years:", age_in_human_years))
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
# function call
print(paste("Age in dog years:", human_years_to_dog_years(10)))
```

But this will not work, because outside of the function, the variable `age_in_dog_years` does not exist.

```{r function_vars2, error=TRUE}
human_years_to_dog_years <- function(age_in_human_years) {
  age_in_dog_years <- 21 + (4 * (age_in_human_years - 2))
  return(age_in_dog_years)
}
print(paste("Age in human years:", age_in_dog_years))

# function call
print(paste("Age in dog years:", human_years_to_dog_years(10)))
```

:::{.callout-exercise #ex-dog_function}

In your `prac6_exercises.qmd` Quarto document, write a function to convert dog years to human years (the reverse of the above). Round the answer to the nearest whole number.

Apply your function to the following:

* Billy, a human aged 180 dog years
* Ahmed, a human aged 44 dog years
* The `Age_Dog_Years` column of the following data frame of four humans:

```{r human_tibble}
human_data <- tibble(
  Name = c(
    "Aisha",
    "Mateo",
    "Priya",
    "Daniel"
  ),
  Age_Dog_Years = c(76, 222, 239, 123)
)
gt(human_data)
```

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #dog_function_ans}
```{r ex-dog_function_ans1}
dog_years_to_human_years <- function(age_in_dog_years) {
  age_in_human_years <- ((age_in_dog_years - 21) / 4) + 2
  return(round(age_in_human_years))
}

print(paste(
  "Billy is", dog_years_to_human_years(180),
  "human years old"
))
print(paste(
  "Ahmed is", dog_years_to_human_years(44),
  "human years old"
))
```

```{r ex-dog_function_ans2}
human_data_updated <- human_data |>
  mutate(Age_Human_Years = dog_years_to_human_years(Age_Dog_Years))

gt(human_data_updated)
```
:::
:::

## Processing cancer data {#sec-process_cancer_data}

Now we're ready to write a function to process one of the cancer CSV files you have been provided with. 

First, let's just look at one dataset, `data/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv`, without using a function.

We will also need to read a second file, `data/by_type.csv`, which has one row for each cancer type and the following columns:

* Total_Individuals - number of individuals with this cancer type in the study
* Total_Mutations - number of mutations of any type identified in individuals with this cancer type in the study
* Total_Severe_Mutations - number of severe mutations identified in individuals with this cancer type in the study

:::{.callout-exercise #ex-cancer_no_function}
In your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file, write a series of steps (not as a function) to:

* Read the files `data/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv` and `data/by_type.csv` into two data frame variables.
* Perform an `inner_join()` to combine information from the two data frames.
* Filter rows in the joined data frame where the value of `Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count` is equal to 0.
* Add two new columns to the resulting data frame which contain, for each gene:
  + `Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Prop`: The proportion of individuals with this cancer type who have a mutation in this gene.
  + `Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Prop`: The proportion of individuals with this cancer type who have a severe mutation in this gene.
* Store the resulting data frame in a variable `mutations`.
* Save the data frame into a file, `output/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv`.

:::{.callout-answer #ex-cancer_no_function_ans}

Read the files `data/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv` and `data/by_type.csv` into two data frame variables.

```{r read_cancer_df #cancer_no_function_ans1, output=FALSE}
gene_mutation_counts <- read_csv("data/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv")
cancer_type_totals <- read_csv("data/by_type.csv")
```

Perform an `inner_join()` to combine information from the two data frames.

```{r read_cancer_df #cancer_no_function_ans3, output=FALSE}
mutation_merged <- inner_join(
  gene_mutation_counts,
  cancer_type_totals
)
```
Filter rows in the joined data frame where the value of `Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count` is equal to 0.

```{r read_cancer_df #cancer_no_function_ans2}
gene_mutation_filt <- mutation_merged |>
  filter(Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count != 0)
```

Add two new columns to the resulting data frame which contain, for each gene:

* `Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Prop`: The proportion of individuals with this cancer type who have a mutation in this gene.
* `Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Prop`: The proportion of individuals with this cancer type who have a severe mutation in this gene.

Store the resulting data frame in a variable `mutations`.

```{r read_cancer_df #cancer_no_function_ans4}
mutations <- gene_mutation_filt |>
  mutate(
    Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Prop = Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Count / Total_Individuals,
    Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Prop = Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count / Total_Individuals,
  )
```

Save the data frame into a file, `output/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv`.

```{r read_cancer_df #cancer_no_function_ans5}
write_csv(mutations, "output/Brain_Lower_Grade_Glioma.csv")
```
:::
:::

Now, let's combine these steps into a function, which can be run on any of the cancer data frames.

We can add an argument, `cancer_type` to tell the function which cancer type we want to look at.

The `paste0` function is useful to combine the `cancer_type` variable with the paths to our input and output files.

First, let's write a function which just reads the two csv files.

```{r cancer_function1}
process_cancer_df <- function(cancer_type) {
  # Read the two CSV files
  gene_mutation_counts <- read_csv(paste0("data/", cancer_type, ".csv"))
  cancer_type_totals <- read_csv("data/by_type.csv")
}
```

Now, let's add our inner join:

```{r cancer_function2}
process_cancer_df <- function(cancer_type) {
  # Read the two CSV files
  gene_mutation_counts <- read_csv(paste0("data/", cancer_type, ".csv"))
  cancer_type_totals <- read_csv("data/by_type.csv")

  # Merge the data frames
  mutation_merged <- inner_join(gene_mutation_counts, cancer_type_totals)
}
```

We can continue adding steps until all of our data frame processing is within this function.

:::{.callout-exercise #ex-cancer_function}

Write a function named `process_cancer_df` to carry out all the steps from [Exercise 1](@ex-cancer_no_function).  

:::{.callout-note #note-function_extras}

* When you make the output file, you'll need to use your `cancer_type` variable again with the `paste0()` function - e.g. `paste0("output/", cancer_type, ".csv")`
* Add an extra line at the bottom of your function to **return** the resulting data frame: `return(mutations)`

:::

:::{.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-cancer_function_ans}

```{r cancer_function_ans, output=FALSE}
process_cancer_df <- function(cancer_type) {
  # Read the two CSV files
  gene_mutation_counts <- read_csv(paste0("data/", cancer_type, ".csv"))
  cancer_type_totals <- read_csv("data/by_type.csv")

  # Merge the data frames
  mutation_merged <- inner_join(gene_mutation_counts, cancer_type_totals)

  # Filter rows with no severe mutations
  gene_mutation_filt <- mutation_merged |>
    filter(Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count != 0)

  # Add additional columns
  mutations <- gene_mutation_filt |>
    mutate(
      Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Prop = Gene_Individuals_with_Mutations_Count / Total_Individuals,
      Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Prop = Gene_Individuals_with_Severe_Mutations_Count / Total_Individuals
    )

  # Save output
  write_csv(mutations, paste0("output/", cancer_type, ".csv"))

  # Return processed data frame
  return(mutations)
}
```

:::
:::

You should now be able to run your function, let's try with the `Lung_Adenocarcinoma` cancer type.

```{r run_cancer_function, output=FALSE}
mutations_lung_ac <- process_cancer_df("Lung_Adenocarcinoma")
gt(head(mutations_lung_ac))
```

## Review {#sec-summary_0601}

[↑ top](#)

::: {.callout-note #note-summary_0601}

### Summary

* You can define your own functions in R using `function()`.
* Functions have arguments and return values.
* You need to **call** a function in order to run it.
* Variables defined inside functions only exist within those functions.
* You can write functions to automate parts of your analysis.

You have applied these skills to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), writing a function to process cancer mutation data. By automating this analysis, the same function can be used to process data from different cancer types without having to rewrite the analysis each time.
:::

For this part of the practical, the main files you have edited are:
* `prac6_exercises.qmd`
* `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd`
